lessons.title: Synthesis approaches and signal flow
lessons.summary: The main ways synths make sound (subtractive, additive, FM/PM, wavetable, sample-based, physical modelling), the classic subtractive voice, and how mono and poly synths allocate voices.
lessons.body:
A synthesiser is a program (or circuit) that turns *control* information, such as "play note 60, fairly hard", into a stream of audio samples. Every design answers the same two questions:

- **Where does the raw sound come from?** A waveform, a recording, a mathematical model.
- **How is it shaped over time?** Filters, envelopes and modulation.

The different "kinds" of synthesis are mostly different answers to the first question. Before choosing one for your instrument, it helps to know what each costs and what it is good at.

## The main approaches

| Approach | Raw material | Shaped by |
|---|---|---|
| Subtractive | Bright waves (saw, square) | Filters remove harmonics |
| Additive | Many sine waves | Per-partial levels |
| FM / PM | Sines modulating sines | Modulation index |
| Wavetable | Stored single cycles | Scanning through tables |
| Sample-based | Recordings | Pitch shift, envelopes |
| Physical modelling | Model of a vibrating object | Model parameters |

### Subtractive

Start with a waveform rich in harmonics and **remove** what you don't want with a filter. A sawtooth through a low-pass filter whose cutoff falls over time gives the classic "pluck" or brass sound. This is the architecture of the Minimoog and most analogue synths, and it is the one you'll build first in this module because each block is simple and audible.

### Additive

Any periodic sound can be described as a sum of sine waves (the next-but-one lesson shows why). Additive synthesis builds the sound directly from those sines, each with its own frequency and level, often with its own envelope. It gives total control, but a low note can need hundreds of sines per voice, and controlling that many parameters musically is hard.

### FM and PM

In **frequency modulation** one oscillator (the *modulator*) varies the frequency of another (the *carrier*) at audio rate. This creates sidebands at the carrier frequency plus and minus multiples of the modulator frequency, so two sine oscillators can produce a complex spectrum. John Chowning developed it at Stanford from 1967 and Yamaha licensed it; the DX7 (1983) made it famous.

Yamaha's commercial "FM" (the DX7 included) is actually implemented as **phase modulation** (adding the modulator to the carrier's *phase* rather than its frequency). An industry-wide prevalence claim is omitted because no reliable survey of implementations was available for this review. The two are mathematically closely related: phase-modulating with a signal is the same as frequency-modulating with its derivative. A practical advantage of PM is that a modulator with a DC offset only shifts the carrier's phase, whereas in true FM it shifts the carrier's pitch. FM is cheap in CPU but notoriously hard to programme by ear.

### Wavetable

Store a set of single-cycle waveforms (a **wavetable**) and play one back with a phase accumulator, optionally sweeping or crossfading through the set to make the timbre evolve. Wolfgang Palm of PPG developed his multi-wavetable version in the late 1970s (Hal Chamberlin had described table-lookup wavetables in 1977, and Michael McNabb developed a similar idea independently); Waldorf instruments continue Palm's approach. Each table is cheap to play, but high notes alias unless you keep band-limited versions of each table (lesson 4).

### Sample-based

Play back recordings of real sounds, re-pitched by reading them faster or slower, then shape them with envelopes and filters. Realism is excellent; memory use is large, and expressive range is limited to what was recorded. Your Digitakt is a sample-based instrument.

### Physical modelling

Simulate the physics of a string, tube or membrane. The classic small example is **Karplus–Strong**: fill a short delay line with noise and feed it back through a gentle low-pass filter. The loop's length sets the pitch (roughly `fs / f0` samples) and the filter makes high harmonics die first, like a plucked string. Julius O. Smith's *Physical Audio Signal Processing* covers this family in depth.

> [!tip] A reasonable first instrument
> Subtractive is the usual first build because each block (oscillator, filter, amplifier, envelope, LFO) can be built and tested on its own. The project brief suggests a monophonic digital subtractive synth as an option; this module teaches every block it would need without committing you to it.

## The classic subtractive voice

A **voice** is everything needed to play one note. The textbook subtractive voice looks like this:

```diagram
 note pitch
     |
     v
 +-------+   +--------+   +-------+
 |  OSC  |-->| FILTER |-->|  AMP  |--> out
 +-------+   +--------+   +-------+
     ^            ^           ^
     |            |           |
    LFO      filter env    amp env
             (+ velocity)  (gate)
```

- **Oscillator (VCO/DCO):** generates a periodic waveform at the note's pitch.
- **Filter (VCF):** usually a resonant low-pass; its cutoff sets brightness.
- **Amplifier (VCA):** multiplies the signal by a gain, so the note can start and stop.
- **Envelopes:** time-varying control signals started by the key (the *gate*). One drives the amplifier, another typically sweeps the filter cutoff.
- **LFO:** a slow oscillator (below about 20 Hz) that wobbles pitch (vibrato), level (tremolo) or cutoff.

The "V" names come from analogue gear where each block was *voltage controlled*. In software the same structure holds: audio flows left to right, and control signals arrive from below.

Notice there are two kinds of signal. **Audio signals** run at the sample rate and you hear them. **Control signals** (envelopes, LFOs, knob positions, MIDI) change more slowly and steer the audio blocks. Keeping these separate is central to real-time design, as later lessons show.

## Monophonic and polyphonic

A **monophonic** synth has one voice: it plays one note at a time. A **polyphonic** synth has several voices and can play chords. *Paraphonic* designs sit between: several oscillators at different pitches share one filter and amplifier.

### Monophonic: note priority

When you hold two keys on a mono synth, which one sounds? That rule is **note priority**:

- **Last-note priority:** the most recently pressed key wins. Releasing it falls back to a key still held.
- **Low-note** or **high-note priority:** the lowest or highest held key wins.

Last-note priority needs a stack of held notes, otherwise releasing the newest note while an older one is held leaves silence or a stuck note:

```python
class MonoVoice:
    """Last-note priority, note stack."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.held = []

    def note_on(self, n):
        if n in self.held:
            self.held.remove(n)
        self.held.append(n)
        return n            # note to play

    def note_off(self, n):
        if n in self.held:
            self.held.remove(n)
        if self.held:
            return self.held[-1]
        return None         # start release

m = MonoVoice()
print(m.note_on(60), m.note_on(64),
      m.note_off(64), m.note_off(60))
# 60 64 60 None
```

When `note_off` returns a note, the voice glides or jumps back to it; `None` means start the release.

### Polyphonic: voice allocation

A poly synth has a fixed pool of voices (say 4 or 8). The **voice allocator** decides which voice plays each new note:

1. If a voice is free, use it.
2. If all are busy, **steal** one. Common choices: the oldest note, the quietest voice, or a voice already in its release phase.

```python
class PolyAlloc:
    """Free voice first, else oldest."""
    def __init__(self, voices):
        self.note = [None] * voices
        self.start = [0] * voices
        self.t = 0

    def note_on(self, n):
        self.t += 1
        ids = range(len(self.note))
        free = [v for v in ids
                if self.note[v] is None]
        if free:
            v = free[0]
        else:            # steal oldest
            v = min(ids, key=lambda i:
                    self.start[i])
        self.note[v] = n
        self.start[v] = self.t
        return v

    def note_off(self, n):
        for v, x in enumerate(self.note):
            if x == n:
                self.note[v] = None

p = PolyAlloc(2)
print([p.note_on(n) for n in (60, 64, 67)])
# [0, 1, 0]: 67 steals voice 0 from 60
```

This sketch marks a voice free as soon as its key is released, so a voice still sounding its release tail can be reused abruptly. Real allocators track the envelope state, prefer voices that have finished, and fade a stolen voice out over a few milliseconds to avoid a click (lesson 5).

> [!warning] Stuck notes
> Every note-on must eventually be matched by a note-off for the same note, or a voice sounds forever. Handle the MIDI convention that a note-on with velocity 0 means note-off, and give yourself an "all notes off" escape. The project brief lists "no stuck notes" as a success criterion.

## Cost and choice

Polyphony multiplies everything: 8 voices means 8 oscillators, 8 filters and 16 envelopes per sample. On a microcontroller this decides your CPU budget. A mono synth is the smallest complete instrument, and a well-structured mono voice becomes one voice of a poly synth later.

## Key takeaways

- Synthesis methods differ mainly in where the raw sound comes from: filtered rich waves, summed sines, modulated sines, stored cycles, recordings or physical models.
- The subtractive voice is oscillator → filter → amplifier, steered by envelopes and LFOs.
- Audio signals run at the sample rate; control signals steer them more slowly.
- Mono synths need a note-priority rule and a held-note stack; poly synths need a voice allocator and a stealing policy.
- Polyphony multiplies CPU cost per voice.

questions.prompt: In the classic subtractive voice, in what order does the **audio** pass through the main blocks?

options.text: Filter → oscillator → amplifier
options.explanation: The filter needs something to filter. The oscillator is the source, so it must come first.

options.text: Oscillator → filter → amplifier
options.explanation: Correct. The oscillator makes a harmonically rich wave, the filter removes some harmonics, and the amplifier (driven by the amp envelope) sets the level over time.

options.text: Oscillator → envelope → LFO
options.explanation: Envelopes and LFOs are control sources. They steer the audio blocks; the audio itself does not flow through them.

options.text: Amplifier → oscillator → filter
options.explanation: An amplifier before the oscillator has nothing to amplify. This confuses the control path (gain) with the audio path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask what creates sound: the **oscillator**. It is always first.
2. Subtractive synthesis *removes* harmonics, so the **filter** comes next.
3. The **amplifier** multiplies by the amp envelope so the note starts and stops.

```
OSC --> FILTER --> AMP --> out
          ^         ^
       filter env  amp env
```

Envelopes and LFOs sit underneath as control signals, not in the audio chain.

questions.prompt: A preset uses two sine oscillators. The second one, running at an audio frequency, is added to the *phase* of the first, and the result is a bright, bell-like spectrum. Which synthesis approach is this?

options.text: Subtractive
options.explanation: Subtractive starts from a rich wave and filters it. Two pure sines have nothing to remove.

options.text: Additive
options.explanation: Additive sums sines at chosen frequencies. Here one sine modulates another rather than being summed, which creates new sidebands.

options.text: FM/PM
options.explanation: Correct. Audio-rate modulation of a carrier's phase (or frequency) by a modulator creates sidebands at the carrier frequency ± multiples of the modulator frequency. Yamaha's FM instruments, including the DX7, actually implement phase modulation, as do most digital FM designs since.

options.text: Wavetable
options.explanation: Wavetable plays stored single cycles. Nothing here is read from a table of stored waveforms.

questions.workedExample:
1. Two sines, one *modulating* the other at audio rate: that is the signature of FM/PM.
2. Modulating phase rather than frequency is **phase modulation**, which Wikipedia notes is what Yamaha's FM actually implemented.
3. Sidebands appear at `fc ± k·fm`, so a couple of sines yield many partials, which is why FM gives bells and electric pianos cheaply.

questions.prompt: You build a Karplus–Strong plucked string at a 48 kHz sample rate and want a pitch of about 220 Hz. Roughly how long should the delay line be?

options.text: About 22 samples
options.explanation: That would be 48,000 / 22 ≈ 2,182 Hz, a factor of ten too high. Check the division.

options.text: About 218 samples
options.explanation: Correct. The loop length sets the period: 48,000 / 220 ≈ 218 samples. (The loop filter adds a little delay, so precise tuning needs a fractional adjustment.)

options.text: About 220 samples, because length in samples equals frequency in Hz
options.explanation: The length is a *period* in samples, i.e. fs / f0. It only happens to be close to 220 here because 48,000 / 220 ≈ 218.

options.text: About 48,000 samples
options.explanation: That is one second of delay, which would repeat once per second (1 Hz), not 220 times per second.

questions.workedExample:
A plucked-string loop repeats once per trip around the delay line, so the trip time is one period.

```
period = 1 / 220 Hz  = 4.545 ms
samples = 0.004545 * 48000
        = 218.2
```

So about 218 samples. The averaging filter in the loop adds roughly half a sample of delay, which is why accurate tuning uses a fractional delay or a tuning filter.

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's last-note-priority `MonoVoice`, what note is sounding after this sequence?

```
note_on(60)
note_on(64)
note_on(67)
note_off(64)
note_off(67)
```

options.explanation: 67 has just been released, so it is no longer in the held stack.

options.text: None (release starts)
options.explanation: Note 60 is still held. Silence here would be the classic bug of a mono synth with no note stack.
64 was released before 67, so it is gone from the stack.
Correct. After both releases the stack is [60], so the voice falls back to the oldest note still held.

questions.workedExample:
Track the stack (top on the right):

```
on 60    [60]          plays 60
on 64    [60, 64]      plays 64
on 67    [60, 64, 67]  plays 67
off 64   [60, 67]      still 67
off 67   [60]          back to 60
```

Releasing 64 while 67 is on top changes nothing audible. Releasing 67 exposes 60, so the voice returns to 60 (with or without a glide, depending on the design).

questions.prompt:
Using the lesson's `PolyAlloc(3)` (free voice first, otherwise steal the oldest), which voices do the last two note-ons get?

```
on 60, on 64, on 67
off 64
on 72
on 76
```

options.text: 72 → voice 1, 76 → voice 0
options.explanation: Correct. Releasing 64 frees voice 1, which 72 takes. For 76 all voices are busy, so it steals the oldest start time: voice 0 (note 60).

options.text: 72 → voice 3, 76 → voice 4
options.explanation: There are only three voices (0, 1, 2). The allocator never creates voices; it reuses or steals them.

options.text: 72 → voice 0, 76 → voice 1
options.explanation: Voice 0 is still playing 60 when 72 arrives, and a free voice (1) is preferred over stealing.

options.text: 72 → voice 1, 76 → voice 1
options.explanation: Voice 1 is now the newest note (72), so 'steal oldest' will not choose it.

questions.workedExample:
```
t1 on 60 -> v0   [60, -, -]
t2 on 64 -> v1   [60, 64, -]
t3 on 67 -> v2   [60, 64, 67]
off 64           [60, -, 67]
t4 on 72 -> v1   free voice
t5 on 76 -> all busy
  start times v0=1 v1=4 v2=3
  oldest = v0 -> steal 60
```

Answer: 72 on voice 1, 76 on voice 0. A real allocator would also fade voice 0 out briefly before reusing it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are **control** signals rather than audio signals in a typical subtractive voice? Select all that apply.

options.text: The MIDI note-on velocity
options.explanation: Correct. Velocity is a single number per note that scales other parameters such as level or cutoff.

options.text: The filter's output
options.explanation: The filtered waveform is audio on its way to the amplifier.

options.text: The amplitude envelope
options.explanation: Correct. It is a slowly varying gain curve that steers the amplifier; you don't listen to it directly.

options.text: A 5 Hz LFO routed to pitch
options.explanation: Correct. At 5 Hz it is far below the audible range of pitch and acts as a control that wobbles the oscillator frequency.

options.text: The oscillator's sawtooth output
options.explanation: That is the audio source itself, running at the sample rate.

questions.workedExample:
Sort each item by asking: *would I hear this if I sent it straight to the speaker?*

| Signal | Kind |
|---|---|
| Amp envelope | control (steers gain) |
| 5 Hz LFO | control (steers pitch) |
| Velocity | control (one number per note) |
| Saw output | audio |
| Filter output | audio |

Control signals can be updated less often than audio, which matters for CPU use (lesson 7).

questions.prompt: Your synth works with your keyboard, but with another controller some notes keep sounding after you let go. A MIDI monitor shows that controller sends a note-on with velocity 0 when a key is released. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The controller is faulty and should send note-off messages instead
options.explanation: Note-on with velocity 0 is an established MIDI convention for note-off. Valid senders use it, so the receiver must handle it.

options.text: The synth's handler treats every note-on as a new note, including velocity 0, so the matching note never ends
options.explanation: Correct. By MIDI convention a note-on with velocity 0 means note-off. Treat it exactly like a note-off for that note.

options.text: The amplitude envelope's release time is too long
options.explanation: A long release fades a note over seconds; it does not keep notes sounding forever while other notes stop normally.

options.text: The voice allocator does not have enough voices
options.explanation: Too few voices causes notes to be *stolen* (cut off), the opposite of notes that never stop.

questions.workedExample:
1. Symptom: notes from one controller never stop. So note-ends are being lost.
2. The monitor shows the 'end' arrives as note-on, velocity 0.
3. The MIDI 1.0 specification allows this as a note-off (it lets senders use running status efficiently).
4. Fix in the handler:

```
if status is NOTE_ON and vel == 0:
    handle_note_off(note)
```

Also keep an 'all notes off' path for recovery.

questions.prompt: On your target board, one mono voice (oscillator, filter, two envelopes, LFO) measures 7% of the audio-callback time budget. Shared output effects take another 12%. If cost scales linearly with voices, what is the largest voice count that stays under a 75% safety ceiling?

options.text: 10 voices
options.explanation: 10 × 7% + 12% = 82%, which exceeds the 75% ceiling.

options.text: 8 voices
options.explanation: Correct. 8 × 7% + 12% = 68% (fits); 9 voices would be 75% exactly, with no margin below the ceiling, and 10 would be 82%.

options.text: 9 voices
options.explanation: 9 × 7% + 12% = 75%, which is *at* the ceiling rather than under it. Leaving no margin defeats the purpose of a safety ceiling.

options.text: 4 voices
options.explanation: 4 voices use only 40% of the budget. It's safe but not the largest count that fits.

questions.workedExample:
Budget = voices × per-voice + shared.

```
8 * 7 + 12 = 68  under 75: ok
9 * 7 + 12 = 75  at ceiling: no
10* 7 + 12 = 82  over
```

So 8 voices. Keep headroom below 100% because measurements vary and the callback must never miss a deadline.

questions.prompt: A paraphonic synth has four oscillators but one shared filter and one shared filter envelope that retriggers on each new key. You hold a three-note chord, then add a fourth note. What happens?

options.text: Only the new note gets a fresh filter sweep; the held notes are unaffected
options.explanation: That would need a filter and envelope per note, i.e. true polyphony. Here the filter is shared.

options.text: The fourth note is silent because paraphonic synths are monophonic
options.explanation: Paraphonic synths *can* sound several pitches at once; what they lack is per-note filtering and amplitude shaping.

options.text: The shared filter envelope restarts, so all four notes get the new filter sweep together
options.explanation: Correct. With one filter and one envelope for all voices, any retrigger affects every sounding note. This is the key audible difference from true polyphony.

options.text: The synth steals the oldest oscillator and the chord drops a note
options.explanation: With four oscillators and four notes there is no need to steal.

questions.workedExample:
1. Paraphonic: several oscillators at different pitches, but **one** filter (and often one amplifier/envelope) shared by all.
2. A new key retriggers that single envelope.
3. All audio passes through the same filter, so every note gets the new sweep.

In a true poly synth each voice has its own filter and envelopes, so only the new voice sweeps. This is why paraphonic chords sound 'glued' and articulations can't differ per note.

questions.prompt: You are improving the lesson's simple `PolyAlloc`. Which changes are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: When stealing, ramp the stolen voice's level to zero over a few milliseconds before starting the new note
options.explanation: Correct. Jumping a sounding voice straight to a new note is a discontinuity, heard as a click. A brief fade removes it.

options.text: Allocate a new voice object on the heap for each note-on to avoid stealing entirely
options.explanation: Unbounded voices break the CPU budget, and allocating memory inside the audio path is unsafe for real-time code. Fixed pools exist for exactly this reason.

options.text: If the same note is struck again while still sounding, it can reuse its own voice
options.explanation: Correct. Retriggering the same voice avoids two copies of one pitch stacking up and is a common policy.

options.text: Prefer a voice whose envelope has fully finished before taking one that is still in its release tail
options.explanation: Correct. A finished voice is silent, so reusing it is inaudible. Taking a releasing voice cuts its tail short.

questions.workedExample:
Think about what the listener hears and what the CPU can afford.

1. Reusing a silent voice: inaudible. Best.
2. Reusing a releasing voice: cuts a tail. Acceptable fallback.
3. Stealing a held voice: audible, so fade it first (a few ms).
4. Same-note retrigger: reuse its voice.
5. Never grow the pool at run time: CPU cost is per voice, and real-time code must not allocate.

A typical priority: idle → releasing (quietest first) → oldest held.

questions.prompt: You must choose a synthesis approach for a first instrument on a small microcontroller with limited RAM. You want classic analogue-style basses and leads and you want to learn each building block. Which choice best fits, and why?

options.text: Sample-based, because playback is the cheapest CPU operation
options.explanation: Playback is cheap in CPU, but recordings need lots of memory, and you'd learn little about oscillators or filters.

options.text: Additive with 200 partials per voice, because it can make any sound
options.explanation: It can in principle, but hundreds of sines per voice is costly and very hard to control musically. Not suited to a first build on a small device.

options.text: Subtractive, because a few simple blocks give the target sounds and each block can be built and tested alone
options.explanation: Correct. A band-limited oscillator, a resonant low-pass, two envelopes and an LFO produce classic basses and leads, fit in small memory, and decompose into testable exercises.

options.text: Physical modelling, because it has the lowest memory use of any method
options.explanation: Some models are small (Karplus–Strong), but physical models target acoustic instruments, not analogue basses and leads, and tuning them is subtle.

questions.workedExample:
Match the requirements one at a time:

| Need | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Analogue-style bass/lead | subtractive |
| Little RAM | not sample-based |
| Learn each block | subtractive |
| Low CPU per voice | not big additive |

Subtractive satisfies all four. Other methods can be added later as oscillator types inside the same voice structure.

lessons.title: Oscillators and the phase accumulator
lessons.summary: How a digital oscillator keeps track of phase across audio blocks, turns frequency into a phase increment, shapes sine, saw, square, triangle and pulse waves, wraps phase correctly and avoids precision drift.
lessons.body:
An oscillator's job sounds trivial: output a repeating waveform at a chosen frequency. The interesting part is *state*. Audio arrives in blocks (say 32 or 48 samples at a time), the frequency may change between or within blocks, and the oscillator must continue exactly where it left off. Get the state wrong and you hear clicks, buzzes and detuning.

Nearly every digital oscillator is built on one idea: the **phase accumulator**.

## Phase as a fraction of a cycle

Represent **phase** as a number in `[0, 1)`: how far through the current cycle you are. 0 is the start of a cycle, 0.5 is halfway, and 1.0 wraps back to 0.

Each sample, advance the phase by the **phase increment**:

```
inc = f / fs        (cycles per sample)
```

At `fs = 48,000` Hz and `f = 440` Hz, `inc = 0.0091667`. After about 109 samples (48,000 / 440) the phase has gone round once, so the output repeats 440 times per second.

A waveform is then just a function of phase:

```python
import math

def sine(p):
    return math.sin(2 * math.pi * p)

def saw(p):              # rises -1 -> 1
    return 2.0 * p - 1.0

def square(p):
    return 1.0 if p < 0.5 else -1.0

def pulse(p, width):     # 0 < width < 1
    return 1.0 if p < width else -1.0

def tri(p):         # -1 at 0, +1 at 0.5
    return 1.0 - 4.0 * abs(p - 0.5)
```

Separating "where am I in the cycle?" from "what value is there?" is what makes the design flexible: the same accumulator drives a sine, a wavetable lookup or an LFO.

```diagram
phase  0 ...... 0.5 ...... 1|0 ...
saw   -1  rises   0  rises  +1|-1
square +1 +1 +1 | -1 -1 -1  |+1
tri   -1   up   +1   down   -1
```

### Pulse width

A **pulse** wave is high for a fraction `width` of each cycle. At 0.5 it is a square wave. Narrower widths sound thinner and more nasal; **pulse-width modulation** (sweeping the width with an LFO) gives a chorus-like movement. Avoid widths of exactly 0 or 1: the wave becomes a constant (DC) and goes silent.

## State carried across blocks

Here is a minimal oscillator that processes a block at a time. The phase lives in the object, not in the function:

```python
import math

class Osc:
    def __init__(self, fs):
        self.fs = fs
        self.phase = 0.0  # cycles, [0,1)

    def process(self, freq, n):
        inc = freq / self.fs
        out = []
        for _ in range(n):
            w = 2 * math.pi * self.phase
            out.append(math.sin(w))
            self.phase += inc
            if self.phase >= 1.0:
                self.phase -= 1.0
        return out

osc = Osc(48000)
a = osc.process(1000, 64)
b = osc.process(1000, 64)     # next block
print(round(osc.phase, 6))
print(round(a[-1], 4), round(b[0], 4))
```

Output:

```
0.666667
0.9239 0.866
```

After 128 samples at 1 kHz, the phase is `128 × 1000 / 48000 = 2.6667` cycles, so 0.6667 after wrapping. The last sample of block A and the first of block B are consecutive points on the same sine.

> [!warning] The block-boundary bug
> If `phase` were a local variable reset to 0 in each `process` call, every block would restart the waveform. At a 64-sample block size that is a discontinuity 750 times a second (48,000 / 64), heard as a buzz at 750 Hz on top of the tone. The roadmap's first oscillator exercise exists to make you get this right.

## Frequency control

Musical pitch is exponential: each octave doubles the frequency. MIDI note numbers convert with the 12-tone equal temperament formula (from module 1):

```
f = 440 * 2 ** ((note - 69) / 12)
```

Note 60 (middle C) is 261.63 Hz. Pitch modulation, pitch bend and detune are added in *semitones* or *cents* before this conversion, then the increment is recomputed. Because the increment is just `f / fs`, it can change every sample without any glitch: the phase simply advances faster or slower from wherever it is.

## Wrapping the phase correctly

When the phase passes 1.0, **subtract 1**. Don't reset it to 0.

Setting it to 0 discards the fraction that overshot, so each cycle becomes a whole number of samples long. That quietly detunes the oscillator:

```python
fs, f = 48000, 1100
inc = f / fs

def mean_period(reset_to_zero, cycles=1000):
    p, n, wraps = 0.0, 0, 0
    while wraps < cycles:
        p += inc
        n += 1
        if p >= 1.0:
            wraps += 1
            if reset_to_zero:
                p = 0.0
            else:
                p -= 1.0
    return n / cycles   # samples/cycle

for r in (True, False):
    T = mean_period(r)
    print(r, round(T, 3), round(fs / T, 1))
```

```
True 44.0 1090.9
False 43.637 1100.0
```

Resetting to zero makes every 1100 Hz cycle exactly 44 samples, giving 1090.9 Hz: about 14 cents flat, an audible error. Subtracting 1 keeps the fraction, so cycle lengths vary between 43 and 44 samples and average out to exactly the right pitch.

Two more wrapping cases matter:

- **Increment of 1 or more** (a very high frequency or extreme modulation): a single subtraction is not enough. Use `p = p - floor(p)`.
- **Negative increments** (through-zero FM, reversed playback): the phase can go below 0, so wrap upwards too. `p - floor(p)` handles both directions. Beware that some languages' remainder operators (such as C's `fmod`) return negative results for negative inputs.

## Integer phase accumulators

Hardware and many embedded libraries use an unsigned 32-bit integer for phase, where the full range 0 to 2³² − 1 represents one cycle. Integer overflow then *is* the wrap, for free and with no drift:

```
inc  = round(f * 2**32 / fs)
phase = (phase + inc) mod 2**32
index = phase >> (32 - table_bits)
```

The frequency resolution is `fs / 2³²`, about 0.000011 Hz at 48 kHz. This is the **numerically controlled oscillator** at the heart of direct digital synthesis (DDS) chips, and the PJRC Teensy Audio Library's waveform object uses a `uint32_t` phase accumulator in the same way (source checked 2026-10-04).

## Floating-point precision drift

Single-precision `float` has a 24-bit significand, about 7 significant decimal digits. That matters in two ways.

**Wrapped phase in float is fine.** Running a float32 accumulator at 440 Hz for a simulated minute gave 439.99972 Hz on average, an error of about 0.001 cents. The phase stays below 1, where floats are precise.

**Unwrapped phase in float is a bug.** If you never wrap (or compute `sin(2π·f·n/fs)` from a growing sample counter `n`), the number grows, and floats get coarser as they grow. The increment gets rounded to the coarse spacing:

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f = 48000, 440.0
inc = np.float32(f / fs)
p = np.float32(0.0)          # never wrapped
for sec in range(1, 301):
    for _ in range(fs):
        p = np.float32(p + inc)
    if sec in (1, 10, 60, 300):
        step = np.float32(p + inc) - p
        hz = float(step) * fs
        print(sec, round(hz, 1))
```

| Time running | Effective pitch |
|---|---|
| 1 s | 439.5 Hz |
| 10 s | 445.3 Hz |
| 60 s | 468.8 Hz |
| 300 s | 375.0 Hz |

The note goes audibly out of tune within seconds and wildly wrong after a few minutes. A drone or a held pad would expose this on stage. Always keep phase wrapped to one cycle (or use the integer form).

## From oscillator to instrument

A practical oscillator also needs:

- **Band-limiting** for saw, square and pulse, or high notes alias badly (lesson 4).
- **Smoothed or per-sample frequency** so pitch changes don't step audibly (lesson 5).
- A **reset policy**: resetting phase on each note-on gives a consistent attack; free-running sounds more like analogue oscillators. Both are valid choices.

Libraries such as DaisySP (`Oscillator`) and the Teensy Audio Library (`AudioSynthWaveform`) provide band-limited waveforms and a way to set or reset phase. Neither smooths frequency changes for you (both simply recompute the increment when you set a new frequency, as checked in their source on 2026-10-04), so smoothing remains your job. The roadmap suggests writing your own sine oscillator first, then comparing with a library's.

## Key takeaways

- Store phase as a fraction of a cycle and advance it by `f / fs` per sample.
- Phase is state: keep it in the oscillator object so blocks join seamlessly.
- Wrap by subtracting 1 (or `p - floor(p)`), never by resetting to 0, which detunes.
- Waveforms are functions of phase; pulse width sets the high fraction of the cycle.
- Unbounded float phase loses precision and drifts badly; wrapped float or 32-bit integer accumulators are stable.

lessons.title: Harmonics, spectra and timbre
lessons.summary: Why a sawtooth sounds different from a square or triangle at the same pitch, the 1/n and 1/n² harmonic patterns that define them, and how to check them yourself with numpy's FFT.
lessons.body:
Play a sine, a triangle, a square and a sawtooth at the same pitch and loudness. Each sounds clearly different: the sine pure, the triangle soft, the square hollow, the saw buzzy and bright. Pitch and loudness are equal, so the difference is **timbre**, and for steady periodic tones timbre is largely set by the **spectrum**: which frequencies are present, and how strong each one is.

This lesson gives you the spectra of the standard waveforms and a way to verify them. Every later block (band-limiting, filters) is easier to reason about in these terms.

## Fourier series: any periodic wave is a sum of sines

A waveform that repeats every `T` seconds, at frequency `f0 = 1/T`, can be written as a sum of sine waves at whole-number multiples of `f0`:

```
x(t) = DC + Σ A_n·sin(2π·n·f0·t + φ_n)
       n=1,2,3...
```

- `DC` is the mean value (zero for the centred waveforms here).
- `n = 1` is the **fundamental**; perceived pitch need not equal the strongest component.
- `n = 2, 3, 4...` are the **harmonics** (or overtones) at 2f0, 3f0, 4f0...
- `A_n` is each harmonic's **amplitude**, and `φ_n` its **phase**.

This is the **Fourier series**. Intuitively: a sine is the only waveform with a single frequency, so anything more complicated must be several sines added together. The sharper the features of a waveform (corners, jumps), the more high harmonics it needs to build them.

The *magnitudes* `A_n` plotted against frequency form the **magnitude spectrum**: a row of spikes at multiples of `f0`, each with a height.

## The standard waveforms

| Wave | Harmonics present | Amplitude of n |
|---|---|---|
| Sine | 1 only | — |
| Saw | all (1, 2, 3...) | 1/n |
| Square | odd (1, 3, 5...) | 1/n |
| Triangle | odd (1, 3, 5...) | 1/n² |

For waves swinging between −1 and +1, the standard series are:

```
saw:  (2/π)  * Σ ±sin(n·ω·t) / n
      all n, alternating sign
square: (4/π) * Σ sin(n·ω·t) / n
      odd n
tri:  (8/π²) * Σ ±sin(n·ω·t) / n²
      odd n, alternating sign
```

(ω = 2π·f0, with time measured from a zero crossing of the wave. The alternating signs are phases; they shape the waveform but not the magnitude spectrum. The sign of the saw series depends on whether it ramps up or down.)

What this means for the sound:

- **Saw** has every harmonic, falling at 6 dB per octave of harmonic number (each doubling of `n` halves the amplitude). This is the brightest standard wave and the usual starting point for subtractive brass, strings and basses.
- **Square** has only odd harmonics at the same 1/n rate. Missing even harmonics give its hollow, woody, clarinet-like character.
- **Triangle** also has only odd harmonics, but they fall at 1/n², i.e. 12 dB per octave. The 3rd harmonic is 1/9 of the fundamental (−19 dB), so it sounds close to a sine.

> [!note] Pulse waves
> A pulse of width `w` has harmonic amplitudes proportional to `|sin(π·n·w)| / n`. Wherever `n·w` is a whole number, that harmonic vanishes. At `w = 0.5` all even harmonics vanish (a square). At `w = 0.25` every 4th harmonic vanishes. This is why sweeping pulse width changes the timbre so audibly.

## Check it with numpy

The roadmap asks you to compare spectra with an existing analysis tool rather than writing an FFT. numpy's `rfft` computes the discrete Fourier transform of a real signal.

A useful trick: analyse exactly **one second** at an **integer** frequency. Then the FFT bins are exactly 1 Hz apart and every harmonic lands exactly on a bin, so there is no leakage to worry about.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f0 = 48000, 100
n = np.arange(fs)                # 1 s
p = (f0 * n / fs) % 1.0          # phase
waves = {
  "saw": 2 * p - 1,
  "square": np.where(p < 0.5, 1.0, -1.0),
  "tri": 1 - 4 * np.abs(p - 0.5),
}
for name, x in waves.items():
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / len(x)
    amps = X[f0 * np.arange(1, 8)]  # bin=Hz
    print(name, np.round(amps / amps[0], 3))
```

Output (harmonics 1 to 7, relative to the fundamental):

```
saw [1. 0.5 0.333 0.25 0.2 0.167 0.143]
square [1. 0. 0.333 0. 0.2 0. 0.143]
tri [1. 0. 0.111 0. 0.04 0. 0.02]
```

(Spacing tidied to fit; values unchanged.) The 1/n, odd-only and 1/n² patterns appear exactly. The absolute fundamental amplitudes come out as 0.6366, 1.2732 and 0.8106, matching 2/π, 4/π and 8/π² from the series.

Note the scaling: `rfft` returns sums, so multiplying by `2 / N` converts a bin to the amplitude of a sine (the factor 2 accounts for the energy split between positive and negative frequencies). For non-integer frequencies or real recordings, apply a window (e.g. `np.hanning`) before the FFT and expect peaks to spread across neighbouring bins.

## Phase changes shape, not (much) timbre

Two waves can have identical magnitude spectra but different shapes. Build a 39-harmonic saw-like tone twice: once with all harmonics in sine phase, once all in cosine phase.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f0 = 48000, 100
t = np.arange(fs) / fs

def build(phase):
    x = np.zeros(fs)
    for n in range(1, 40):   # 39 harmonics
        x += np.sin(2*np.pi*n*f0*t
                    + phase) / n
    return x

for ph in (0.0, np.pi / 2):  # sin vs cos
    x = build(ph)
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / fs
    print(np.round(X[[100, 200, 300]], 3),
          round(np.abs(x).max(), 2))
```

```
[1.    0.5   0.333] 1.81
[1.    0.5   0.333] 4.25
```

Same harmonic amplitudes, but the cosine-phase version has a peak 2.3 times higher (about 7.4 dB), because all its harmonics line up at t = 0. For steady tones the ear is much more sensitive to the magnitudes than the phases, so the two sound very similar. Your **headroom** does not care what it sounds like: the peak is what clips. Filters change phases, which is one reason a filtered signal can peak higher than its input.

## Gibbs ripple

Adding up a finite number of harmonics never quite produces a perfect corner. A square wave built from odd harmonics overshoots each jump by about 9% of the jump size, however many harmonics you add (peaks of about 1.18 for a ±1 square). This is the **Gibbs phenomenon**. It matters later: a *band-limited* square or saw, the kind that doesn't alias, has these ripples by construction. They are correct, not a bug.

## Timbre is more than the static spectrum

The spectrum explains why waveforms differ, but real timbre also depends on how the spectrum **changes over time**. A piano's high harmonics die faster than its fundamental; a brass note gets brighter as it gets louder. That is why synths pair oscillators with filters, envelopes and modulation, which change the spectrum while the note plays. The DSP learning objectives ask you to describe a target sound in exactly these terms: pitch, spectrum, envelope and modulation.

## Key takeaways

- A periodic wave consists of its DC mean plus sinusoids at multiples of its fundamental; their magnitudes form its spectrum.
- Saw: all harmonics at 1/n. Square: odd at 1/n. Triangle: odd at 1/n². Pulse: zeros where n·w is whole.
- Use `np.fft.rfft`, one second of signal and integer frequencies to read harmonic amplitudes exactly; scale by 2/N.
- Phase changes the waveform's shape and peak level, which matters for headroom, while changing the steady timbre little.
- Band-limited jumps ripple (Gibbs); timbre also depends on how the spectrum evolves over time.

- [Timbre — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre)

questions.prompt: Which description matches the spectrum of an ideal square wave?

options.text: All harmonics, amplitude 1/n
options.explanation: That is the sawtooth. The square's symmetry cancels every even harmonic.

options.text: Odd harmonics only, amplitude 1/n²
options.explanation: That is the triangle, whose harmonics fall much faster.

options.text: Odd harmonics only, amplitude 1/n
options.explanation: Correct. 1, 3, 5, 7... at 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental. The missing evens give the hollow sound.

options.text: Only the fundamental
options.explanation: That is a sine wave; a square has sharp jumps that need many harmonics.

questions.workedExample:
From the Fourier series `(4/π) Σ sin(nωt)/n` over odd n:

```
n:    1   2   3    4   5
amp:  1   0   1/3  0   1/5
```

Odd only, falling as 1/n. Compare the triangle (odd, 1/n²) and saw (all, 1/n).

questions.prompt: A sawtooth plays at 200 Hz. How strong is its 600 Hz component relative to the fundamental, in dB?

options.text: About −9.5 dB
options.explanation: Correct. 600 Hz is the 3rd harmonic; saw harmonics fall as 1/n, so 1/3, and 20·log10(1/3) ≈ −9.5 dB.

options.text: About −19 dB
options.explanation: That is 1/9 (1/n²), the triangle rule, not the saw.

options.text: 0 dB, because all harmonics are equally loud
options.explanation: A saw's harmonics get weaker with n. Equal-strength harmonics would describe an impulse train.

options.text: It is absent, because saws contain only odd harmonics
options.explanation: The *square* lacks even harmonics. A saw has all of them, and in any case 3 is odd.

questions.workedExample:
1. Harmonic number: 600 / 200 = **3**.
2. Saw amplitude rule: 1/n = **1/3**.
3. In dB: 20·log10(1/3) = **−9.54 dB**.

questions.prompt: Why does a triangle wave sound much closer to a sine than a square wave does, even though both contain only odd harmonics?

options.text: The triangle has fewer harmonics than the square
options.explanation: Both have infinitely many odd harmonics in the ideal case. The difference is how fast they fall.

options.text: Its harmonics fall as 1/n², so the 3rd is only 1/9 (−19 dB) and the 5th 1/25 (−28 dB) of the fundamental
options.explanation: Correct. The fundamental dominates far more than in the square, where the 3rd is 1/3 (−9.5 dB).

options.text: A triangle's harmonics are out of phase with each other, which cancels them
options.explanation: The alternating signs are phases; they affect the shape, not the magnitude of each harmonic.

options.text: A triangle has only even harmonics, which blend with the fundamental
options.explanation: A triangle has *odd* harmonics, the same set as a square.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the 3rd and 5th harmonics:

| | 3rd | 5th |
|---|---|---|
| Square (1/n) | −9.5 dB | −14 dB |
| Triangle (1/n²) | −19 dB | −28 dB |

The triangle's energy is overwhelmingly in the fundamental, so it sounds soft and nearly pure.

questions.prompt: You run `np.fft.rfft` on **24,000** samples recorded at 48 kHz. Which output index holds the 300 Hz component?

options.explanation: That's true only when the analysis is exactly one second long (1 Hz bins). Here the bins are 2 Hz apart.
That would be the case with 2 seconds of audio (0.5 Hz bins). Half a second gives wider bins.
Correct. Bin spacing = fs / N = 48000 / 24000 = 2 Hz, so 300 Hz is at index 300 / 2 = 150.
That is N/2, the index of the Nyquist frequency (24 kHz).

questions.workedExample:
```
bin spacing = fs / N
            = 48000 / 24000 = 2 Hz
index = f / spacing = 300 / 2 = 150
```

General rule: index = f · N / fs. This is why the lesson uses exactly one second: indices equal hertz.

questions.prompt: A pulse wave has width w = 1/3. Using the rule that harmonic amplitude is proportional to |sin(π·n·w)| / n, which harmonics are missing?

options.text: All even harmonics (2, 4, 6...)
options.explanation: That's what happens at w = 1/2, the square wave.

options.text: Every 3rd harmonic (3, 6, 9...)
options.explanation: Correct. sin(π·n/3) = 0 whenever n is a multiple of 3.

options.text: None; only a square wave has missing harmonics
options.explanation: Any width that is a simple fraction makes some harmonics vanish.

options.text: Harmonics 1, 2 and 3 only
options.explanation: The fundamental is never zero for 0 < w < 1; sin(π/3) ≈ 0.87.

questions.workedExample:
Check n = 1..6 with w = 1/3:

```
n  n·w   sin(π·n·w)
1  1/3   0.87
2  2/3   0.87
3  1     0
4  4/3  -0.87  (abs 0.87)
5  5/3  -0.87
6  2     0
```

Zeros at n = 3, 6, 9... So sweeping width moves these 'holes' through the spectrum, which is what pulse-width modulation sounds like.

questions.prompt: You analyse exactly one second (48,000 samples) of a 1 kHz sine with amplitude 0.5. What raw magnitude does `abs(np.fft.rfft(x))[1000]` return, before any scaling?

options.explanation: That is the value *after* scaling by 2/N. The raw FFT is an unnormalised sum.
That would be the magnitude for amplitude 1.0 (N/2). With amplitude 0.5 it is half that.
That is N; a sine's magnitude is split across positive and negative frequencies, so it's N·A/2.
Correct. Raw magnitude = N·A/2 = 48000 × 0.5 / 2 = 12,000. Multiplying by 2/N recovers 0.5.

questions.workedExample:
1. The DFT sums N samples, so a full-scale sine gives magnitude proportional to N.
2. A real sine's energy is shared between +f and −f bins, so each gets half: N·A/2.
3. 48000 × 0.5 / 2 = **12,000**.
4. To read amplitude: 12000 × 2 / 48000 = **0.5**.

questions.prompt: A 1 kHz sawtooth is generated at a 48 kHz sample rate. How many of its harmonics (including the fundamental) lie **below** the 24 kHz Nyquist frequency?

options.explanation: The 24th harmonic is at 24 kHz exactly, which is not *below* Nyquist.
Correct. Harmonics are at 1, 2, ..., 23 kHz below Nyquist. The 24th sits exactly on it and higher ones are above it.
That would be the count for odd harmonics only (a square), and even then it's 12 below 24 kHz: 1, 3, ..., 23.

options.text: Infinitely many
options.explanation: The ideal saw has infinitely many harmonics, but the question asks how many fit below Nyquist.

questions.workedExample:
```
harmonic k is at k * 1000 Hz
k * 1000 < 24000  ->  k < 24
k = 1 .. 23       ->  23 harmonics
```

Everything from the 24th up cannot be represented; the next lesson shows what happens if a naive oscillator generates it anyway (aliasing).

questions.prompt: Which statements about spectra and timbre are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: For steady tones, the ear is far more sensitive to harmonic magnitudes than to their phases
options.explanation: Correct. That is why the two phase versions sound very similar.

options.text: Two waveforms with identical harmonic magnitudes but different phases can look very different on a scope
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson's sine-phase vs cosine-phase example had the same spectrum but peaks of 1.81 vs 4.25.

options.text: Sharper waveform corners need fewer harmonics
options.explanation: The reverse: sharp corners and jumps need many high harmonics.

options.text: A sound's timbre is fully described by one static magnitude spectrum
options.explanation: Timbre also depends on how the spectrum changes over time (attack, decay of harmonics), which is why envelopes and filters matter.

options.text: The pitch we hear for a saw is normally its fundamental frequency
options.explanation: Correct. Harmonics at integer multiples fuse into one note at f0.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against the lesson:

- Phase changes shape and peak: **true**.
- Ear mostly ignores phase on steady tones: **true**.
- Pitch = fundamental for harmonic sounds: **true**.
- Static spectrum = whole timbre: **false**; evolution over time matters.
- Sharp corners = fewer harmonics: **false**.

questions.prompt: You normalise a patch so a sine-phase additive saw peaks at 0.9. You then add a phase-shifting effect that leaves every harmonic's *amplitude* unchanged, and the output starts clipping. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The effect added new harmonics above Nyquist, which alias and raise the level
options.explanation: A phase-only change adds no new frequencies, so nothing new can alias.

options.text: The phase shift lined up harmonic peaks more closely, raising the waveform's peak even though the spectrum magnitudes are unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. Peak level depends on how harmonics align in time. The lesson saw 1.81 vs 4.25 for the same spectrum (about 7.4 dB).

options.text: Phase shifts always add 3 dB of gain
options.explanation: There is no fixed gain; an all-pass phase change leaves each sine's amplitude the same. The *peak* depends on alignment.

options.text: The FFT shows the same spectrum, so clipping must come from a bug elsewhere
options.explanation: Same magnitude spectrum does not mean same peak. This is a real effect, not necessarily a bug.

questions.workedExample:
1. Magnitudes unchanged, so the RMS (overall energy) is unchanged.
2. Peak = how the harmonics' crests coincide. A phase shift can align more of them.
3. In the lesson, aligning all 39 harmonics (cosine phase) took the peak from 1.81 to 4.25: 20·log10(4.25/1.81) ≈ **7.4 dB**.
4. So a 0.9 peak could become well above 1.0 and clip.

Practical lesson: leave headroom after any filter or phase-altering stage, and measure peaks, not just spectra.

questions.prompt: You generate a properly band-limited square wave (many odd harmonics, scaled by 4/π so the flat parts sit at ±1). Your output stage clips at ±1.0. Roughly what gain should you apply to avoid clipping on its own?

options.text: 1.0, because the square only reaches ±1
options.explanation: The band-limited square overshoots its edges by about 9% of the 2-unit jump (Gibbs), peaking near ±1.18.

options.text: About 0.5, because a square has twice the energy of a sine
options.explanation: Energy is not what clips; the peak is. 0.5 is much more cut than needed.

options.text: About 0.85
options.explanation: Correct. The Gibbs overshoot gives peaks of about 1.18, and 1 / 1.18 ≈ 0.85 brings them to 1.0. In practice you'd go lower still for headroom.

options.text: About 0.64 (2/π)
options.explanation: 2/π relates to the saw's fundamental amplitude; it isn't the right factor for the square's Gibbs peak.

questions.workedExample:
1. Gibbs phenomenon: a finite sum of harmonics overshoots a jump by about 9% of the jump.
2. Jump = 2 (from −1 to +1), so overshoot ≈ 0.18 → peak ≈ **1.18**. Summing odd harmonics up to the 39th, or up to the 199th, both give a peak of about 1.179.
3. Gain to bring 1.18 to 1.0: 1/1.18 ≈ **0.85**.

The overshoot doesn't shrink as you add harmonics; it just narrows.

questions.prompt: You FFT a recording of your synth at 440 Hz and the peaks look smeared across many bins, unlike the lesson's clean output. Which are valid explanations or remedies? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smearing proves the oscillator is aliasing
options.explanation: Aliasing produces extra *discrete* peaks at folded frequencies, not general smearing. Leakage and modulation explain smearing.

options.text: If the note has an envelope or vibrato, the spectrum genuinely changes during the window
options.explanation: Correct. A time-varying sound can't produce one sharp spectrum; analyse shorter windows or a steady section.

options.text: Apply a window such as `np.hanning` before the FFT to reduce leakage
options.explanation: Correct. Windowing tapers the ends of the segment, trading slightly wider peaks for much lower leakage.

options.text: Multiply the FFT output by 2/N to remove the smearing
options.explanation: That scaling converts magnitudes to amplitudes; it doesn't change the shape of the spectrum.

options.text: 440 Hz over your analysis length is not a whole number of cycles, so energy leaks into neighbouring bins
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson's trick (one second, integer Hz) puts every harmonic exactly on a bin. Otherwise you get leakage.

questions.workedExample:
Separate *measurement* effects from *signal* effects:

1. Leakage: non-integer cycles in the window. Remedy: window, or choose the length to fit whole cycles.
2. Time variation: envelopes and vibrato spread energy. Remedy: analyse a steady segment.
3. Aliasing appears as distinct peaks at non-harmonic frequencies, not smearing.
4. 2/N scaling only changes units.

lessons.title: Band-limited oscillators
lessons.summary: Why naive saw and square oscillators alias, worked out with real numbers, and the established fixes (additive, mipmapped wavetables, oversampling, BLIT, BLEP and PolyBLEP), with a measured PolyBLEP-versus-naive comparison in Python.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson showed that a sawtooth has harmonics at every multiple of its fundamental, forever. A digital system at sample rate `fs` can only represent frequencies below `fs/2`. Module 1 covered what happens to anything above: it **aliases**, folding back to a different frequency.

The naive oscillator from lesson 2, `2*p - 1`, samples an ideal saw directly. It therefore contains all those impossible harmonics, and they fold back into the audible band. This lesson puts numbers on the problem and shows how real synths solve it.

## Where the harmonics go

Take a high-ish note: `f0 = 1245 Hz` (close to D#6) at `fs = 48 kHz`. Nyquist is 24 kHz, so harmonics 1 to 19 (up to 23,655 Hz) are fine. Harmonic 20 is at 24,900 Hz and folds back:

```
folded = |f - k*fs|  for the nearest k

h20: 24900 -> 48000 - 24900 = 23100
h21: 26145 -> 48000 - 26145 = 21855
h31: 38595 -> 48000 - 38595 =  9405
h38: 47310 -> 48000 - 47310 =   690
h39: 48555 -> 48555 - 48000 =   555
```

| Harmonic | Lands at | Level (1/n) |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 23,100 Hz | −26.0 dB |
| 31 | 9,405 Hz | −29.8 dB |
| 38 | 690 Hz | −31.6 dB |
| 39 | 555 Hz | −31.8 dB |

Two things make this bad:

- **The aliases are not harmonic.** 9,405 Hz and 690 Hz are not multiples of 1245 Hz, so they sound like dissonant, metallic tones rather than brightness.
- **They move the wrong way.** Bend the pitch up and a real harmonic rises, but a folded one can *fall*. Pitch sweeps produce the tell-tale "birdie" whistles moving against the note.

A component 30 dB down is clearly audible, especially at 690 Hz, where the ear is sensitive and there is little of the real tone nearby to mask it. Low notes suffer less, because their harmonics are already weak (1/n is small) by the time they reach Nyquist.

> [!note] Why square waves are no better
> The naive square has the same 1/n odd harmonics, so it aliases just as badly. A naive triangle is much better (1/n² falls faster), and a sine has nothing to alias. The problem is **discontinuities**: an instantaneous jump contains energy at all frequencies.

## Established fixes

There is no free lunch. Each method trades CPU, memory, latency or flexibility.

### 1. Additive synthesis

Sum only the harmonics below Nyquist: for this note, harmonics 1 to 19. The result is perfectly band-limited by construction. The cost is one sine per harmonic per sample: a 50 Hz note at 48 kHz has 479 harmonics below Nyquist. Fine offline, expensive for a polyphonic synth on a microcontroller.

### 2. Band-limited wavetables (mipmaps)

Precompute single-cycle tables using additive synthesis, offline. Keep several versions: one per octave (say), each containing only the harmonics that stay below Nyquist for the **highest** note that table will play. At playback, choose the table for the current pitch and read it with a phase accumulator and interpolation.

```
table for notes up to 2 kHz:
  harmonics < 24000 / 2000: max 11
table for notes up to 1 kHz:
  harmonics < 24: max 23
table for notes up to 500 Hz:
  harmonics < 48: max 47
```

This is cheap per sample and works for any waveform, which is why wavetable synths use it. The costs are memory, a slight loss of brightness at the bottom of each table's range, and possible audible switching between tables (crossfading helps). Some designs deliberately allow harmonics that fold back *above* 20 kHz, keeping more brightness at the cost of some inaudible aliasing.

### 3. Oversampling

Run the naive oscillator at a multiple of the sample rate (say 4× or 8×), low-pass filter, then discard samples (decimate). Aliases still occur, but they fold around the higher Nyquist and most of their energy is filtered out. Simple to reason about, costly in CPU, and the decimation filter must be good.

### 4. BLIT: band-limited impulse train

Stilson and Smith (CCRMA, 1996) generate a band-limited train of impulses using a closed-form formula, then **integrate** it to get a saw (or integrate a bipolar impulse train for a square). It's elegant and accurate, though the integrators need care to avoid DC drift.

### 5. BLEP and PolyBLEP: correct the jumps

Insight: a saw is smooth everywhere *except* at its jump. Aliasing comes from the jumps. So generate the naive wave, then **add a correction** around each discontinuity that turns the ideal step into a band-limited step.

- **minBLEP** (Eli Brandt, 2001) precomputes a band-limited step, makes it minimum-phase, and stores the difference from an ideal step in a table. At each jump, the oscillator adds the table, aligned to the jump's exact fractional position.
- **PolyBLEP** (Välimäki and Huovilainen, 2007) replaces the table with a tiny polynomial that only touches two samples: the one just before the jump and the one just after it. It is cheap and needs no memory, at the cost of weaker suppression than a long table.

```diagram
naive saw          PolyBLEP saw
    /|  /|             /\  /\
   / | / |            /  \/  \
  /  |/  |           /        \
 jump: 1 sample      jump spread over
 (aliases)           ~2 samples
```

## A PolyBLEP saw in Python

The polynomial below is the widely circulated two-sample PolyBLEP (as used in Martin Finke's tutorial). `t` is the phase in `[0, 1)` and `dt` the phase increment:

```python
import numpy as np

def poly_blep(t, dt):
    # t: phase [0,1), dt: increment
    if t < dt:             # just after jump
        t = t / dt
        return t + t - t * t - 1.0
    if t > 1.0 - dt:       # just before
        t = (t - 1.0) / dt
        return t * t + t + t + 1.0
    return 0.0

def saw(f0, fs, n, blep):
    dt, p = f0 / fs, 0.0
    out = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        y = 2.0 * p - 1.0
        if blep:
            y -= poly_blep(p, dt)
        out[i] = y
        p += dt
        if p >= 1.0:
            p -= 1.0
    return out

fs, f0 = 48000, 1245     # 1 s: bin = 1 Hz
k = np.arange(fs // 2 + 1)
harm = (k % f0 == 0) & (k > 0)
low = (k > 0) & (k < 10000)
for blep in (False, True):
    x = saw(f0, fs, fs, blep)
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / fs
    alias = np.where(~harm & low, X, 0)
    w = np.argmax(alias)
    db = 20 * np.log10(alias[w] / X[f0])
    h10 = 20 * np.log10(X[10 * f0] * 10
                        / X[f0])
    print("polyblep" if blep else "naive",
          w, round(db, 1), round(h10, 1))
```

Output:

```
naive 9405 -29.8 0.0
polyblep 9405 -55.4 -1.9
```

Reading it: the strongest alias below 10 kHz is at 9,405 Hz in both cases (harmonic 31 folded), but PolyBLEP pushes it from −29.8 dB to −55.4 dB relative to the fundamental, an improvement of about 25 dB. The last column is the 10th harmonic (12,450 Hz) relative to its ideal 1/n level: PolyBLEP softens it by 1.9 dB. In the same run the 19th harmonic (23.7 kHz) was 7.6 dB low. That is PolyBLEP's trade-off: it gently dulls the very top octave while removing most of the audible aliasing.

The saw's jump is downwards (+1 to −1), so the correction is *subtracted*. A square has a rising jump at phase 0 and a falling one at the pulse width `w`, so it needs two corrections:

```
y = 1 if p < w else -1
y += poly_blep(p, dt)
y -= poly_blep((p - w) mod 1, dt)
```

A quick check with the same analysis gave −55.4 dB worst alias below 10 kHz for both `w = 0.5` and `w = 0.3` (naive: −29.8 and −28.7 dB). Remember that a pulse with `w ≠ 0.5` also has a DC offset of `2w − 1`, which you may want to remove.

Triangle waves have corners, not jumps. They can be corrected with a band-limited *ramp* (BLAMP), or made by integrating a PolyBLEP square with a leaky integrator, which is what DaisySP's `WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI` does.

## Using a library

You don't need to invent any of this. As of 2026-10-04 (GitHub master branches; confirm against current documentation):

- **DaisySP** `Oscillator` offers naive waveforms plus `WAVE_POLYBLEP_SAW`, `WAVE_POLYBLEP_SQUARE` and `WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI`.
- **Teensy Audio Library** `AudioSynthWaveform` offers `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH`, `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH_REVERSE`, `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SQUARE` and `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_PULSE` alongside the naive ones. Its source (`synth_waveform.cpp`, class `BandLimitedWaveform`) inserts a precomputed band-limited step from a lookup table at each edge, interpolated to the edge's fractional position and spread across a window of about 32 samples (16 either side of the edge): a table-based BLEP approach, not PolyBLEP.

The roadmap exercise is exactly this lesson's experiment: generate naive and band-limited versions at a high pitch, run them through the FFT analysis, and listen to a slow upward sweep of each.

## Choosing a method

| Method | CPU | Memory | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Additive | high | low | exact; costly for low notes |
| Mipmapped tables | low | medium | any waveform |
| Oversampling | high | low | needs a good decimator |
| PolyBLEP | low | none | some top-end droop |
| minBLEP | medium | small table | better suppression |

For a first subtractive voice on a microcontroller, PolyBLEP is the usual pragmatic choice.

## Key takeaways

- Naive saw and square waves alias because their jumps contain energy above Nyquist; the folded components are inharmonic and move against pitch bends.
- Fold-back frequency is `|f − k·fs|`; at 1245 Hz and 48 kHz, harmonic 31 lands at 9,405 Hz about 30 dB down.
- Fixes: additive, mipmapped wavetables, oversampling, BLIT, minBLEP and PolyBLEP.
- PolyBLEP corrects two samples around each jump; in the test it cut the worst low alias by about 25 dB while softening the top harmonics slightly.
- Libraries (DaisySP, Teensy Audio) already provide band-limited waveforms; compare them with naive ones as an exercise.

## Further reading

- [Stilson and Smith, Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms (BLIT, PDF)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)
- [Brandt, Hard Sync Without Aliasing (minBLEP, PDF)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~eli/papers/icmc01-hardsync.pdf)
- [Martin Finke, PolyBLEP Oscillator](https://www.martin-finke.de/articles/audio-plugins-018-polyblep-oscillator/)
- [DaisySP Oscillator header (GitHub)](https://github.com/electro-smith/DaisySP/blob/master/Source/Synthesis/oscillator.h)
- [Teensy Audio Library — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_Audio.html)
- [Teensy Audio Library waveform source, synth_waveform.cpp (GitHub)](https://github.com/PaulStoffregen/Audio/blob/master/synth_waveform.cpp)
- [Välimäki and Huovilainen, Antialiasing Oscillators in Subtractive Synthesis (Aalto research portal)](https://research.aalto.fi/en/publications/antialiasing-oscillators-in-subtractive-synthesis/)
- [Spectral Audio Signal Processing — Julius O. Smith, CCRMA](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/)

questions.prompt: What feature of a naive sawtooth (`2*p - 1`) is the root cause of its aliasing?

options.text: Its linear ramp
options.explanation: A straight ramp on its own is smooth; it's the reset at the end of each ramp that causes trouble.

options.text: Its instantaneous jump from +1 to −1, which contains energy at all frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. A discontinuity needs infinitely many harmonics. Sampling it directly folds everything above Nyquist back down.

options.text: Its amplitude of ±1
options.explanation: Scaling the wave changes the level of the aliases, not whether they exist.

options.text: Using floating point instead of integers
options.explanation: An integer implementation of the same naive wave aliases identically. It's a sampling problem, not a number-format one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Lesson 3: sharp features need many high harmonics; a jump needs all of them (1/n forever).
2. Anything above fs/2 cannot be represented, so it folds back (module 1).
3. The ramp is harmless; correct the jump (BLEP) or never create it (additive, wavetables) and the aliasing goes.

questions.prompt: A naive saw plays at 2,500 Hz with fs = 48 kHz. Where does its 19th harmonic end up, and roughly how loud is it relative to the fundamental?

options.explanation: 47.5 kHz can't exist at a 48 kHz sample rate; it must fold below 24 kHz.

options.text: It is simply removed because it is above Nyquist
options.explanation: Nothing removes it: a naive oscillator samples the ideal wave, so the harmonic folds back instead of disappearing.

options.text: 500 Hz at about −25.6 dB
23,500 Hz at about −25.6 dB
options.explanation: That would be reflecting around Nyquist from 24,500 Hz. Use |f − k·fs|: 47,500 is close to 48,000, so it lands near 0.

questions.workedExample:
```
f   = 19 * 2500 = 47500 Hz
fold: nearest multiple of fs = 48000
      |47500 - 48000| = 500 Hz
level = 1/19 -> -25.6 dB
```

A 500 Hz tone under a 2.5 kHz note is not a multiple of it, so it sounds like a clashing low whistle.

questions.prompt: Why are aliased components from a naive oscillator so much more objectionable than the same amount of extra brightness?

options.text: They are louder than the fundamental
options.explanation: Usually they are well below it (around −26 to −32 dB in the lesson's example). Level isn't the main issue.

options.text: They only occur in square waves
options.explanation: Saws alias equally; triangles less; sines not at all.

options.text: They are inharmonic and move in the wrong direction when the pitch changes
options.explanation: Correct. Folded components aren't multiples of the fundamental, so they clash, and on a pitch sweep some fall while the note rises.

options.text: They increase the DC offset
options.explanation: Aliasing produces tones at folded frequencies, not a DC shift.

questions.workedExample:
Real harmonics: k·f0, all rise together with pitch.

Aliases: |k·f0 − m·fs|. When k·f0 is just below m·fs, raising f0 *lowers* the alias.

So a sweep up produces whistles sweeping down ('birdies'). That motion and inharmonicity make even −30 dB aliases obvious.

questions.prompt: You build mipmapped saw tables at fs = 48 kHz with no aliasing allowed. One table serves notes up to 3.5 kHz. What is the highest harmonic it may contain?

options.explanation: Correct. Harmonic h of a 3.5 kHz note is at 3500·h, which must stay below 24 kHz: 24,000 / 3,500 ≈ 6.86, so h ≤ 6 (the 6th is at 21 kHz; the 7th would be 24.5 kHz).
That uses fs (48 kHz) instead of fs/2: 48,000 / 3,500 ≈ 13.7. Harmonics up to 45.5 kHz would alias badly.

options.text: `y -= poly_blep(p, dt)` only
options.explanation: That's the saw correction. A pulse has two jumps per cycle, at 0 and at w.

options.text: `y += poly_blep(p, dt); y -= poly_blep((p - w) % 1, dt)`
options.explanation: Correct. Rising edge at phase 0 (add), falling edge at phase w (subtract), with the second BLEP evaluated on the phase relative to w. The lesson measured −55.4 dB worst low alias for w = 0.3 with this.

y += blep(p, dt)

questions.prompt: Which methods reduce aliasing during oscillator generation or before final downsampling, rather than merely attenuating output afterwards? Select all that apply.

options.text: Switch to mipmapped band-limited wavetables
options.explanation: Correct. Each table contains only harmonics that stay below Nyquist for its note range.

options.text: Put a 10 kHz low-pass filter after the oscillator
options.explanation: A post-filter can remove aliases above 10 kHz, but cannot separate aliases below its cutoff from wanted sound. It is not prevention during generation.

options.text: Add PolyBLEP corrections at both the rising and falling edges
options.explanation: Correct. This band-limits both jumps; the lesson measured about 25 dB less low-frequency aliasing.

options.text: Turn the oscillator's output level down
options.explanation: Aliases scale with the signal; their level relative to the note doesn't change.
